title: Hydrazine-Assisted Reductive Leaching of Zinc Cake: Thermodynamic Assessment, RSM Optimization, and Microstructural Evolution of Refractory Residues
abstract: Abstract Ferrite–silicate zinc leach residues are notoriously difficult to process hydrometallurgically—largely because ZnFe 2 O 4  remains stable even under aggressive sulfuric acid conditions. This work presents, for the first time, a systematic study of hydrazine (N 2 H 4 ) as a selective reductant for treating zinc cake generated at the Almalyk Mining and Metallurgical Complex (AMMC), Uzbekistan. Thermodynamic calculations over 25–120 °C confirmed that hydrazine readily reduces Fe(III) to Fe(II) within the ferrite lattice: Δ G ° values reached −860.8 and −608.7 kJ mol −1  for zinc and copper ferrites at 25 °C, and became more negative as the temperature rose. This Fe(III) → Fe(II) conversion disrupts the spinel structure, rendering it soluble in dilute H 2 SO 4 . Four leaching variables—acid concentration, hydrazine dosage, temperature, and time—were systematically evaluated using central composite design (CCD) coupled with response surface methodology (RSM). All four fitted models showed  R 2  > 0.98 and  p  < 0.05, with temperature and hydrazine consumption identified as the dominant factors for Zn recovery. Under the RSM-derived optimum (1.0 M H 2 SO 4 , 6.3 wt.% N 2 H 4 , 85 °C, 2 h), extract ion efficiencies of 91.7% Zn, 98.1% Cu, 91.2% Cd, and 85.6% Fe were achieved experimentally, alongside a 55–60% reduction in solid residue mass. Post-leach X-ray diffraction (XRD) showed that readily soluble zinc phases were almost fully consumed, whereas anglesite (PbSO 4 ), willemite (Zn 2 SiO 4 ), and residual ZnFe 2 O 4  survived selectively in the solid. High-resolution TEM and STEM-EDS analyses revealed dramatic particle fragmentation: the original ~74 µm feed agglomerates broke down to 0.9–2.0 µm fragments through preferential dissolution along ferrite–silicate grain boundaries. Importantly, hydrazine oxidized cleanly to N 2  and H 2 O only—no CO 2  or problematic solid byproducts were detected. Residual hydrazine in process effluents was neutralized below regulatory discharge limits (< 0.01 mg L −1 ) by H 2 O 2  treatment. Taken together, these results establish hydrazine-assisted reductive leaching as a thermodynamically grounded, statistically optimized, and environmentally viable route for recovering valuable metals from zinc metallurgical waste. Graphical Abstract Zinc cake valorization: Decomposition of ZnFe 2 O 4  using hydrazine, process optimization by RSM, and residue analysis

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The recovery of valuable metals from metallurgical residues has gained considerable industrial and scientific momentum over the past two decades, driven by the progressive depletion of high-grade primary ore reserves and tightening regulatory constraints on industrial waste disposal [ 1 ,  2 ]. Zinc cake—the filter residue generated after sulfuric acid leaching of oxidatively roasted zinc sulfide concentrates—exemplifies the class of secondary materials that warrant particular attention within this context. It carries appreciable concentrations of zinc, copper, cadmium, and lead, yet simultaneously qualifies as hazardous industrial waste under most national and international classification schemes. Recovering these metals in a technically credible and environmentally defensible manner is therefore both an industrial priority and a scientific challenge of broad relevance to nonferrous hydrometallurgy.

Efforts to process zinc-bearing residues of this kind span both pyrometallurgical and hydrometallurgical domains. On the pyrometallurgical side, sodium carbonate roasting has been the subject of sustained investigation [ 3 ,  4 – 5 ]: its capacity to decompose zinc ferrite through high-temperature solid-state reactions is well established, and various modifications—including the use of secondary additives to suppress iron dissolution during the roasting step [ 4 ]—have been systematically documented. Conventional sulfuric acid leaching, while straightforward in principle, encounters fundamental dissolution barriers when applied to materials rich in refractory zinc phases such as ZnFe 2 O 4  and Zn 2 SiO 4  [ 6 ,  7 ]. A comprehensive review of the hydrometallurgical strategies available for zinc-bearing industrial residues [ 8 ] documents the breadth of the recovery challenge and underscores the absence of a universally satisfactory solution. The zinc cake continuously generated at the Almalyk Mining and Metallurgical Complex (AMMC), Uzbekistan, presents this challenge in particularly acute form. Characterization of this material reveals a mineralogically complex phase assemblage in which a substantial fraction of the total zinc inventory is distributed among chemically resistant phases—principally zinc ferrite (ZnFe 2 O 4 ), zinc silicate (Zn 2 SiO 4 ), and residual zinc sulfide—none of which dissolves to any practically useful extent under the acid concentrations and temperatures that conventional industrial leaching can realistically sustain. More targeted approaches have therefore been developed and evaluated. Jiang et al. [ 9 ] demonstrated a novel multistage route for recovering metals from hydrometallurgical zinc residues, while Ju et al. [ 10 ] reported a clean aqueous pathway for jarosite-type residues carrying zinc, copper, and cadmium. The mechanistic role of reductant selection in destabilizing the zinc ferrite spinel lattice was examined by Kazemi and Sichen [ 11 ], who showed that Fe(III) → Fe(II) conversion—achieved in their study using carbon and hydrogen—is a necessary prerequisite for subsequent acid dissolution. Parallel work on organic acid-mediated leaching demonstrated that citric acid can achieve extraction efficiencies approaching those of mineral acid routes under milder conditions when applied to AMMC zinc cake [ 12 ]. The hydrometallurgical extraction of zinc from zinc ferrite using acidic lixiviants was systematically characterized by Leclerc et al. [ 13 ], and high-pressure sulfuric acid leaching was established as an effective route for silica-rich zinc oxide ores resistant to ambient-pressure treatment [ 14 ]. The broader sustainability context for these recovery efforts is well articulated in the circular economy literature [ 15 ]: transitions in resource-intensive industries depend not only on technical innovation but also on institutional conditions that incentivize secondary material use. Among the hydrometallurgical options that have been investigated, alkaline leaching has been explored for selectively recovering zinc and lead from mixed-metal waste streams [ 16 ], and sequential hydrometallurgical processing has been shown to recover lead and silver alongside zinc from complex leach residues [ 17 ,  18 ]. Solvent-free aqueous routes combining selective acid dissolution and precipitation have achieved satisfactory zinc and lead co-recovery from industrial leach residues [ 19 ]. On the pyrometallurgical side, sulfate roasting represents a thermochemical alternative [ 20 ], while the Waelz kiln remains the most widely deployed industrial technology for zinc-bearing waste processing—its dominance reflecting both proven zinc recovery rates of 85–90% and decades of continuous process refinement [ 21 ,  22 ]. Microwave-assisted pressure leaching has demonstrated energy efficiency advantages for complex concentrates [ 23 ], and solvent extraction using D2EHPA has been established as a viable downstream step for recovering zinc from pregnant leach solutions [ 24 ]. More recently, calcium roasting coupled with ammonia leaching was reported as a selective method for zinc ferrite decomposition [ 25 ], and pressure leaching in sulfuric acid has shown effectiveness for zinc silicate-bearing ores [ 26 ]. Within the AMMC context specifically, Yakubov et al. [ 27 ] described a hydrometallurgical flowsheet for zinc cake processing that underscores the industrial urgency of improving reductive leaching strategies for this material. None of these routes is without significant drawbacks. In hydrometallurgical flowsheets, iron co-dissolution is a persistent headache: it forces multistage solution purification—typically jarosite, goethite, or hematite precipitation—before electrolysis can proceed, and each of these steps produces its own iron-bearing solid waste requiring long-term management. Pyrometallurgical routes carry analogous burdens; the Waelz process leaves behind iron-rich slag and carries substantial energy costs, while roasting-based options still demand involved solution purification prior to electrowinning. Reductive leaching with water-soluble organics such as citric acid or glucose has been explored as a gentler middle path [ 12 ,  27 ]. These reagents do work, but their relatively large molecules diffuse slowly to reactive mineral surfaces—a kinetic limitation that becomes more pronounced as particle size decreases. There is also a more fundamental issue: Biomass-derived reductants such as coffee shell have been shown to achieve iron oxide decomposition at elevated temperatures, but require high-temperature processing (700 °C) and generate carbon-containing byproducts [ 28 ]. Their oxidative breakdown produces CO 2 , which sits awkwardly alongside the decarbonization commitments that modern metallurgical operations are increasingly expected to meet. Against this backdrop, hydrazine hydrate (N 2 H 4 ·H 2 O) stands out as a reductive agent whose physicochemical profile is unusually well matched to the demands of zinc ferrite dissolution—yet it has received virtually no systematic attention in this application. Three properties are worth noting. Its molecular weight of 32.05 g mol −1  permits rapid diffusion to reactive mineral surfaces, sidestepping the kinetic bottleneck that hampers bulkier organic reductants. Its complete miscibility with water ensures uniform distribution through a leaching slurry, eliminating the concentration gradients that can compromise reproducibility. And its only oxidation products are molecular nitrogen and water—there is no CO 2  pathway whatsoever—representing a genuine process-level advantage over organic reductants whose oxidation generates CO 2 . However, industrial hydrazine production via the Raschig process carries a significant upstream carbon footprint (estimated 4.5–8.2 kg CO 2 -eq kg −1  product); a complete life-cycle assessment would be required to establish the net carbon profile of this approach, and is recommended as a direction for future environmental evaluation. Whether hydrazine can, in practice, address the kinetic, thermodynamic, and environmental shortcomings of previously studied reductants for AMMC-specific zinc cake is a question the open literature has not answered. No published work has established the thermodynamic feasibility of hydrazine-mediated ZnFe 2 O 4  decomposition, and no study has reported practical extraction efficiencies for this particular material. There is also a methodological gap: the integration of response surface methodology (RSM)-based statistical optimization with high-resolution microstructural characterization has not been applied to this class of residue in a single experimental framework. RSM implemented via central composite design (CCD) allows the individual and interactive effects of multiple process variables to be quantified simultaneously, with far fewer experimental runs than classical one-variable-at-a-time approaches, while delivering statistically robust optimization outcomes [ 29 ]. The present study was therefore designed with three interrelated objectives: to establish the thermodynamic basis for hydrazine-mediated Fe(III) reduction in the ZnFe 2 O 4  lattice and characterize the subsequent acid dissolution behavior of the resulting oxide intermediates; to identify—through RSM/CCD—the leaching conditions that simultaneously maximize Zn, Cu, and Cd extraction from AMMC zinc cake while limiting Fe co-dissolution; and to 
characterize, through X-ray diffraction (XRD) and  high-resolution transmission electron microscopy/scanning transmission electron microscopy coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (TEM/STEM–EDS), the microstructural evolution of the leach residue under optimized conditions. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this represents the first integrated study of hydrazine-assisted reductive leaching applied to AMMC zinc cake, and the outcomes are intended to provide both mechanistic insight and a practically viable, environmentally credible basis for improving metal recovery from zinc production residues at industrial scale.

sections.heading: Raw Material Acquisition and Sample Preparation
paragraphs: Zinc cake samples were sourced directly from the operating zinc production line at the AMMC, Uzbekistan. The material is a hydrometallurgical residue that accumulates after sulfuric acid leaching of oxidatively roasted zinc sulfide concentrates processed in fluidized-bed furnaces. Sampling was deliberately carried out upstream of the industrial water-washing stage—a decision driven by the need to preserve soluble phases that would otherwise be partially stripped during that step, thereby maintaining the native mineralogical and chemical state of the cake as it exits the leach circuit. Upon receipt, the material was dried at 80 °C under forced-air convection until constant mass was achieved—typically within 24 h—then mechanically homogenized by rotary tumbling to reduce compositional heterogeneity between subsamples. The homogenized cake was stored in sealed polyethylene containers until further use. All 29 CCD experimental runs and the three RSM validation experiments were conducted using aliquots drawn from this single homogenized batch to eliminate inter-batch compositional variability as a confounding factor. Batch-to-batch variability in AMMC zinc cake composition was not formally quantified in this study; based on the continuous nature of the AMMC zinc production circuit and published data for comparable operations, major-element variability is expected to be typically < 5% relative—substantially larger than the within-batch reproducibility demonstrated by the CCD center-point replicates (Zn range: 0.4%, relative standard deviation [RSD]: 0.22%).

Before each leaching experiment, portions of the dried cake were ground in a laboratory ball mill and classified by wet sieving to a top particle size of 74 µm (−200 mesh). This size fraction was chosen to provide consistent surface area exposure across all experimental runs and to suppress interparticle diffusion resistance as a variable that could obscure the effects of the chemical parameters under investigation.

sections.heading: Chemical and Mineralogical Characterization of the Feed Material
Elemental Composition by Energy-Dispersive X-ray Fluorescence (EDXRF)
paragraphs:
Bulk elemental composition was determined by energy-dispersive X-ray fluorescence spectrometry, using an Axios-mAX instrument (Malvern Panalytical, UK) equipped with a rhodium X-ray tube and operated at 60 kV and 125 mA. Sample preparation followed a binder-free pelletizing protocol: dried powder was uniaxially pressed into 40 mm diameter pellets at 20 t to achieve sufficient mechanical integrity while avoiding any dilution or contamination of the matrix that a binder would introduce. This approach was considered important given the heterogeneous multiphase nature of the material, where even minor matrix modification can distort intensity ratios for heavier elements such as Pb and Zn. Quantitative analysis relied on fundamental parameter calibration referenced against certified multi-element standards. The resulting elemental and oxide weight fractions are compiled in Tables  1  and  2 , respectively; the corresponding EDXRF spectrograms are shown in Figs.  1  and  2 .

The EDXRF results reveal a markedly heterogeneous polymetallic system. Zinc is the principal metal of interest at 17.30 wt.%, but the matrix is far from simple: lead (11.80 wt.%) and sulfur (9.90 wt.%) are present at concentrations that rival zinc on a mass basis, while silicon (6.24 wt.%) signals a substantial siliceous gangue fraction inherited from the original ore. Iron (5.71 wt.%), calcium (2.69 wt.%), copper (1.32 wt.%), manganese (1.18 wt.%), and aluminum (1.02 wt.%) contribute at levels that are nontrivial from both a mineralogical and a process chemistry standpoint. What makes this material particularly complex—and commercially interesting—is the co-occurrence of these major constituents with a suite of economically significant trace species. Cadmium (0.46 wt.%), arsenic, zirconium, and the noble metals silver and gold are detectable, each reflecting a different aspect of the material's solid-state history: sulfide oxidation during fluidized-bed roasting, partial dissolution in the preceding leach circuit, and selective concentration of refractory or low-solubility phases in the cake; trace Pt- and Ir-bearing phases are identified by XRD (Table  3 ), but their EDXRF-reported concentrations are excluded from Tables  1  and  2  owing to spectral interference with the Zn-Kβ emission line.

sections.heading: Mineralogical Characterization by XRD
paragraphs: Phase identification was carried out by powder X-ray diffraction on a Bruker D8 Advance diffractometer using Cu Kα radiation ( λ  = 1.5406 Å). Patterns were collected over a 2θ range of 10°–80° with a step size of 0.02° and a dwell time of 1 s per step. All measurements were performed at the Department of Metallurgy, Almalyk State Technical Institute. Observed reflections were matched against the International  Centre for Diffraction Data (ICDD) Powder Diffraction File PDF-4+ reference database using Bruker EVA software. Quantitative phase abundances were extracted by Rietveld refinement in TOPAS 6.0. The refinement strategy included simultaneous adjustment of scale factors, unit cell parameters, crystallite size (modeled via the Lorentzian broadening term), and preferred orientation corrections where diffraction intensities deviated from the calculated pattern in a systematic way. Convergence was assessed by monitoring the weighted profile R-factor alongside visual inspection of the difference curve. The resulting quantitative phase composition is reported in Table  3 .

Rietveld refinement confirms a phase assemblage of considerable mineralogical complexity, consistent with a zinc hydrometallurgical residue that has undergone partial—but incomplete—processing through the roasting and leaching circuit. Sulfate phases dominate the bulk composition. Anglesite (PbSO 4 ) accounts for 17.3 wt.%, and a family of zinc-bearing mixed-cation sulfates—incorporating Cu, Cd, and Ba in variable proportions—contributes a further 18.0 wt.%. Both are straightforward products of extensive sulfation during fluidized-bed roasting, and neither presents a significant dissolution challenge under acidic leaching conditions. The refractory fraction is more consequential. Willemite (Zn 2 SiO 4 , 8.0 wt.%) crystallizes via solid-state reaction between ZnO and siliceous gangue at the elevated temperatures sustained within the roasting furnace. Once formed, it resists dissolution in dilute H 2 SO 4  on thermodynamic grounds—a point developed quantitatively in the section “ Thermodynamic Assessment of Hydrazine-Assisted Reductive Leaching .” Zinc ferrite [(Zn,Cu)Fe 2 O 4 , 6.0 wt.%] precipitates under oxidizing high-temperature conditions and is broadly acknowledged as the most chemically recalcitrant zinc-bearing phase encountered in such residues; its dissolution requires reductive pretreatment rather than straightforward acid attack. Residual marmatite [(Zn,Fe)S, 4.0 wt.%] signals incomplete sulfide oxidation during roasting—an outcome attributable to the particle size distribution of the concentrate feed and to localized thermal gradients inherent to fluidized-bed operation, both of which create zones where oxidation kinetics fall short of completion. Collectively, the zinc inventory distributed across these three phases—ferrite, silicate, and residual sulfide—constitutes the primary metallurgical target of this study. Recovering it requires a processing strategy that goes beyond conventional sulfuric acid leaching, which is precisely the motivation for the reductive leaching approach developed here.

sections.heading: Reagents
paragraphs: Sulfuric acid (H 2 SO 4 , 95–98 wt.%, Sigma-Aldrich, ACS grade) was diluted to the required molar concentrations using deionized water (resistivity ≥ 18.2 MΩ cm, Milli-Q Integral, Merck) immediately before each experimental run. Fresh preparation was enforced as a matter of routine to avoid concentration drift from evaporative losses or atmospheric moisture uptake during storage. Hydrazine hydrate (N 2 H 4 ·H 2 O, 64 wt.%, Sigma-Aldrich, ≥ 98% purity) served as the reductive agent throughout. It was introduced into the reactor after—and separately from—the acid solution in every run. This sequencing was not arbitrary: adding hydrazine to an already-acidified slurry prevents any premature reagent interaction in the feed lines and preserves independent control over both acid concentration and reductant dosage, two variables whose effects on extraction would be confounded if the reagents were premixed. Calibration of the inductively coupled plasma–optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) instrument relied on multi-element standard solutions (Merck Certipur, NIST-traceable), with all dilutions prepared in deionized water. Hydrazine hydrate warrants explicit safety commentary. Under the Globally Harmonized System of Classification and   Labelling of Chemicals (GHS) classification system it carries three hazard designations: acute oral toxicity (Acute Tox. 3), suspected human carcinogenicity (Carc. 1B), and flammable liquid (Flam. Liq. 3). Every operation involving this reagent was therefore confined to a certified fume hood. Personnel wore chemical-resistant gloves, a full face shield, and a flame-retardant laboratory coat at all times, in accordance with institutional chemical safety requirements. Effluent management was handled with equal care. All hydrazine-bearing waste streams were treated in situ by controlled addition of hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 , 30 wt.%) prior to disposal, oxidizing residual hydrazine quantitatively to N 2  and H 2 O. Treated effluents were subsequently analyzed by the  p -dimethylaminobenzaldehyde colorimetric method to confirm that residual hydrazine concentrations fell below the applicable the applicable regulatory discharge limit of 0.01 mg L −1  before release.

At laboratory scale, neutralization was conducted using dilute H 2 O 2  (3 wt.%) added continuously at 50 mL min −1 —a controlled rate that produced no measurable temperature rise, stable solution pH, and gradual N 2  evolution throughout. No signs of runaway reaction were observed. However, the theoretical reaction enthalpy (N 2 H 4  + 2H 2 O 2  → N 2  + 4H 2 O, ΔH ≈ −641 kJ mol −1 ) is significant at industrial scale. Any future scale-up implementation would require (i) dilute H 2 O 2  addition (< 10 wt.%); (ii) controlled addition rate with automatic temperature cutoff at 50 °C; (iii) continuous temperature monitoring; (iv) vented or scrubbed off-gas collection; and (v) explosion-proof electrical classification of the treatment area. Calorimetric characterization under process-relevant conditions is recommended as an essential component of any scale-up feasibility assessment. It is noted that Cu 2+  present in the pregnant leach solution—derived from ktenasite dissolution—may catalyze the H 2 O 2 -mediated oxidation of residual hydrazine through a Fenton-type Fe 3+ /Fe 2+  cycling mechanism [ 30 ], potentially reducing the H 2 O 2  dosage required to achieve the regulatory discharge limit. It should be noted that the claim of N 2  and H 2 O as the exclusive oxidation products is based on thermodynamic analysis and observational evidence—no ammonia odor was detected during any of the 29 CCD runs or validation experiments. However, no dedicated off-gas analysis or solution NH 4 +  quantification was performed, and trace disproportionation to NH 4 +  cannot be entirely excluded. A complete nitrogen mass balance is recommended for future scale-up studies. At industrial scale, implementation of hydrazine-assisted leaching would require (i) confirmation that hydrazine sulfate (N 2 H 6 SO 4 ), the dominant species at pH ≈ 0, poses no explosive hazard at the operating temperature of 85 °C—its decomposition temperature of ~254 °C provides a thermal safety margin exceeding 169 °C; (ii) ATEX-classified process equipment, dedicated UN 2030-compliant storage, closed-loop ventilation with activated carbon scrubbing, and continuous in-line hydrazine monitoring with automated process interlock; and (iii) recognition that the reagent cost premium of hydrazine hydrate relative to organic reductants (~3–5× per kg) is partially offset by simpler effluent treatment and superior trace-element selectivity. A formal techno-economic comparison with organic reductant alternatives is recommended as a priority for future engineering feasibility studies.

sections.heading: Reductive Leaching Procedure
paragraphs: All leaching experiments were carried out in a 500 mL jacketed borosilicate glass reactor. The vessel was equipped with a water-cooled reflux condenser to limit reagent volatilization at elevated temperatures, a calibrated precision thermometer (±0.1 °C), and a polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)-coated magnetic stir bar. Temperature control was achieved by circulating thermostatic fluid through the jacket via a programmable recirculating water bath (Julabo F25-ME, Germany), which held the reaction temperature within ±1 °C of each target value throughout the run. A solid-to-liquid (S/L) ratio of 1:5 g mL −1  was maintained across all experiments. The S/L ratio of 1:5 g mL −1  was not selected arbitrarily; rather, it was determined based on two independently verifiable engineering and analytical constraints: (i) suspension hydrodynamics—engineering assessment of the reactor geometry and feed particle size distribution (< 74 µm) confirmed that 1:5 g mL −1  maintains complete particle suspension at 400 rpm, thereby avoiding settling-induced bias; and (ii) ICP-OES calibration compatibility—at S/L = 1:5, the theoretical Zn concentration (~34.6 g L −1 ) requires only a single 1:50 dilution to fall within the validated calibration range, whereas higher solid loadings would necessitate error-prone serial dilutions. A formal parametric optimization of extraction efficiency as a function of S/L ratio was not conducted in the present study and is recommended as a priority for future scale-up investigation. Each run began with the transfer of a pre-weighed zinc cake aliquot (10.00 ± 0.01 g) into the reactor, which already contained the preheated sulfuric acid solution at the target concentration. The slurry was stirred at 400 rpm for 5 min before hydrazine addition to allow full thermal equilibration between the solid and liquid phases. Hydrazine hydrate was then introduced dropwise through a calibrated glass burette at a deliberate, controlled rate. Slow addition was essential: rapid injection creates transient local excesses of reductant that distort the stoichiometric conditions at the mineral surface during the critical early stage of ferrite reduction. The 400 rpm agitation rate itself had been validated in separate mass transfer experiments to ensure that external liquid-film resistance was not rate-limiting under any of the conditions explored in the main design. At the end of each run, the slurry was vacuum-filtered immediately through a 0.45 µm mixed cellulose ester membrane. The clarified leachate was acidified to 2 vol.% HNO 3  (TraceMetal grade) and refrigerated at 4 °C pending ICP-OES analysis. Solid residues were rinsed three times with 50 mL portions of deionized water, dried at 80 °C to constant mass, and weighed to quantify the overall mass reduction relative to the feed. Every experimental condition was replicated three times, and all reported values represent means ± one standard deviation (SD).

sections.heading: Experimental Design and RSM Optimization
Leachate Analysis and Extraction Efficiency Calculation
Thermodynamic Modeling
paragraphs: The thermodynamic viability of the proposed reaction network was evaluated by computing standard Gibbs free energy changes (Δ G °) and equilibrium constants ( K eq ) over the temperature interval 25–120 °C. Calculations were performed in HSC Chemistry 9.0 (Outotec, Finland), a package whose thermochemical database is well established for oxide, sulfate, and aqueous systems of this type. The thermodynamic stability of the relevant mineral phases and dissolved ionic species under the applied leaching conditions was assessed through the Δ G ° and Keq calculations presented in the section “ Thermodynamic Assessment of Hydrazine-Assisted Reductive Leaching ,” complemented by electrochemical analysis of the key redox couples operative at pH ≈ 0, as discussed below.

sections.heading: Residue Characterization
paragraphs: Phase evolution in the leach residues was tracked by powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) under the same acquisition conditions described in the section “ Mineralogical Characterization by XRD ,” with quantitative phase fractions extracted by semiquantitative Rietveld refinement in TOPAS 6.0. This allowed direct comparison of phase abundance between the feed and the post-leach solid, providing a bulk-averaged picture of which phases were consumed and which survived. Particle morphology and nanoscale compositional heterogeneity were examined by TEM and STEM–EDS, using an FEI Talos F200X instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) operated at 200 kV. Specimen preparation involved ultrasonic dispersion of residue powder in absolute ethanol for 10 min, followed by drop-casting onto holey carbon-coated 300-mesh copper grids and air drying. High-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) imaging was used as the primary STEM mode, exploiting its Z-contrast sensitivity to distinguish compositionally distinct phases without the need for additional staining or contrast enhancement. Simultaneous elemental maps for Zn, Fe, Pb, Si, Mn, Cu, and associated trace elements were collected using the integrated four-detector Super-X EDS system, which provides solid-angle coverage sufficient for reliable quantification at the acquisition currents used.

sections.heading: Thermodynamic Assessment of Hydrazine-Assisted Reductive Leaching
paragraphs:
Before interpreting the experimental extraction data, it is worth establishing what thermodynamics actually permits—and forbids—within this system. The computed Δ G ° values and their temperature dependence for the ten principal reactions are listed in Table  4 ; Fig.  3  plots their trajectories across 25–120 °C, and Fig.  4  presents the corresponding equilibrium constants. The most striking feature of the thermodynamic landscape is the sheer magnitude of the driving force for ferrite reduction. At 25 °C, hydrazine-mediated decomposition of zinc ferrite (Reaction 1) and copper ferrite (Reaction 2) yields Δ G ° values of − 860.8 and −608.7  kJ mol −1 , respectively. Numbers of this magnitude reflect two reinforcing contributions: the strongly exothermic character of Fe(III) → Fe(II) reduction by N 2 H 4 , and the substantial entropic stabilization gained by releasing N 2  as a gaseous product—a thermodynamic benefit that organic reductants, whose carbon is oxidized to CO 2  rather than a diatomic gas, cannot fully replicate. What makes these values particularly significant from a process standpoint is their temperature dependence: both become more negative as temperature rises, meaning the thermodynamic driving force for ferrite decomposition strengthens—rather than erodes—across the experimentally relevant range. This stands in direct contrast to citric acid, glucose, and sucrose, where competing side reactions and CO 2  evolution constrain the useful operating window at elevated temperatures. The oxide intermediates liberated by ferrite reduction—ZnO, CuO, FeO, and CdO, along with Zn(OH) 2  already present in the feed—dissolve readily in dilute H 2 SO 4 . Reactions 3–7 all carry moderately negative Δ G ° values throughout the 25–120 °C window, confirming spontaneity under all practical leaching conditions. A slight upward drift in Δ G ° with temperature is observed for Reactions 4, 5, and 7, reflecting the thermodynamic cost of water solvation at higher temperatures. The effect is real but small—nowhere near sufficient to threaten spontaneity—and can be safely disregarded in process design. Willemite (Zn 2 SiO 4 ) is the single exception. Reaction 8 carries a positive Δ G ° across the entire 25–120 °C range, and this sign does not change. This is not a kinetic argument; it is a thermodynamic one. Dilute sulfuric acid simply cannot dissolve willemite under any temperature condition examined here, and the persistence of this phase in the post-leach residue—documented in the section “ Characterization of Solid Residue under Optimized Leaching Conditions ”—is a direct consequence of this thermodynamic barrier rather than insufficient reaction time or inadequate acid strength. Sulfide dissolution follows a different pattern. Reactions 9 and 10 are already spontaneous at ambient temperature and become progressively more favorable as temperature increases, consistent with the thermally activated mechanism generally accepted for oxidative sulfide dissolution. This trend supports conducting leaching at elevated temperatures even from the perspective of sulfide phase recovery. The equilibrium constant data in Fig.  4  add quantitative weight to these observations.  K eq  values for Reactions 1 and 2 are exceptionally large, indicating that hydrazine-mediated ferrite reduction proceeds essentially to completion under equilibrium conditions. In practice, this means the step is not constrained by thermodynamics—whatever rate limitations exist are kinetic or transport-related, not energetic. For Reaction 8,  K eq  remains below unity across the full temperature range, which is fully consistent with the experimental observation that willemite survives leaching intact regardless of the conditions applied. Taken together, the thermodynamic analysis points to an operating window of 70–85 °C as optimal. Within this range, the driving forces for ferrite reduction and sulfide dissolution are simultaneously maximized, while the energy penalty of operating at higher temperatures remains manageable from a process economics perspective. This range therefore informed the upper boundary of the temperature factor in the subsequent RSM design.

The thermodynamic feasibility of hydrazine-mediated Fe(III) reduction under the acidic leaching conditions is further confirmed by electrochemical analysis. In 1 M H 2 SO 4  (pH ≈ 0), hydrazine exists predominantly as N 2 H 5 +  (pK a  = 8.1), and the relevant N 2 H 5 + /N 2  couple has  E ° = −0.23 V vs. SHE (standard hydrogen electrode) in acidic solution. The overall cell EMF against the Fe 3+ /Fe 2+  couple ( E ° = +0.77 V) is therefore +1.00 V, corresponding to Δ G ° = −386 kJ mol −1 —strongly negative and fully consistent with the HSC-computed values in Table  4 . N 2 (g) is the thermodynamically stable nitrogen product under the applied leaching window (pH ≈ 0, Eh ≈ +0.5 to +0.7 V). The N–H bond dissociation in hydrazine generates reactive hydrogen species that preferentially attack Fe–O bonds in the ferrite lattice, consistent with H• radical attack mechanisms documented in analogous H-transfer systems [ 31 ].

The Pourbaix (Eh–pH) diagrams for the Zn–H 2 O (Fig.  5 a), Fe–H 2 O (Fig.  5 b), Cu–H 2 O (Fig.  5 c), and Cd–H 2 O (Fig.  5 d) systems at 85 °C (358.15 K), constructed using FactSage 8.4 (EpH module), are presented in Fig.  5 . Within the determined leaching operating window (pH 0.5–1.5, Eh −0.15 to +0.20 V vs. SHE), all four metals are situated within their respective aqueous ionic stability domains (Fe 2+ , Zn 2+ , Cu 2+ , and Cd 2+ ), confirming that hydrazine-mediated reductive dissolution effectively maintains these species in solution. Notably, the Fe 3+ /Fe 2+  boundary is located well above this operating window, providing clear electrochemical evidence of the thermodynamic driving force for Fe(III) reduction, which is consistent with the standard Gibbs free energy (Δ G °) calculations presented earlier. sections.heading: RSM/CCD Optimization
paragraphs:
The full experimental matrix—29 runs in total, spanning the factorial, axial, and center-point groups of the CCD—is presented in Table  5  alongside the observed extraction responses for each metal. Three parameters were held fixed throughout: solid-to-liquid ratio at 5 mL g −1 , stirring speed at 400 rpm, and feed particle size at ≤ 74 µm. Their exclusion from the design was deliberate. Preliminary trials had already established that none of these variables exerted a statistically distinguishable effect on extraction within the ranges accessible under the experimental constraints, and fixing them reduced the design to a manageable size without sacrificing the ability to resolve the effects of the four primary chemical and thermal variables. Lead and silver were excluded from the response set for a straightforward chemical reason: under the sulfuric acid concentrations applied across the design, both metals precipitate preferentially as PbSO 4  and Ag 2 SO 4 —phases of sufficiently low solubility that their dissolved concentrations in the leachate do not reflect true extraction in any meaningful sense. Attempting to model their behavior within an RSM framework would therefore produce regression equations that describe sulfate precipitation thermodynamics rather than leaching performance. The analysis was consequently restricted to Zn, Cu, Cd, and Fe, for which solution-phase concentrations are a reliable proxy for extraction efficiency under the conditions applied.

Statistical fit metrics for all four models are compiled in Table  6 . The numbers are, by any standard, strong.  R 2  and adj- R 2  exceed 0.98 and 0.97, respectively, across every response, indicating that the fitted polynomials account for the overwhelming majority of the observed variance without relying on overfitting. Adequate precision values—a signal-to-noise diagnostic specific to Design-Expert, with a threshold of 4.0—range from 31.1 to 1054.9, confirming that the models carry enough discriminating power to be used predictively across the full design space. Predicted versus actual plots (Fig.  6 ) show scatter distributed symmetrically about the parity diagonal with no discernible curvature or trend, which rules out systematic model bias as a concern. The four metals do not behave uniformly, and the model structures reflect this. Zinc extraction is captured adequately by a purely linear model in which all four main effects reach statistical significance at  p  < 0.05. Temperature and hydrazine dosage carry the largest positive coefficients—an outcome that sits comfortably with the thermodynamic picture developed in the section “ Thermodynamic Assessment of Hydrazine-Assisted Reductive Leaching ,” where both variables were shown to reinforce Fe(III) reduction and ferrite lattice destabilization. Cadmium follows a linear model as well, but its response surface has a different shape: a strongly negative slope along the acid concentration axis and a positive one along the hydrazine axis. The former reflects the tendency of Cd 2+  to form poorly soluble sulfate precipitates at high H 2 SO 4  concentrations, effectively removing it from solution before it can be quantified; the latter reflects its partial sequestration within ferrite solid solutions, from which reductive dissolution is required for liberation. Copper and iron both require second-order models, signaling that curvature and interaction effects are non-negligible across the studied parameter space. Copper is, in one sense, the least interesting of the four responses: it achieves near-complete extraction—consistently above 98%—across a wide range of conditions (Fig.  8 ), which is entirely consistent with its mineralogical form in the feed. Ktenasite [(CuZn) 5 (SO 4 ) 2 (OH) 6 ·6H 2 O] and copper sulfate phases dissolve readily even under mild acidic conditions, so the quadratic model for Cu primarily captures the edges of the design space where acid concentration or time becomes limiting. It should be noted that Cu extraction values approaching or exceeding 99% in individual CCD runs (e.g., Run 2: 99.7%) are not statistically distinguishable from complete extraction given the ±3% RSD analytical precision of ICP-OES; they should be interpreted as evidence that Cu recovery is operating near its practical ceiling of ~98–99.5% rather than as genuinely exceeding it. A small fraction of Cu incorporated as a solid solution within the ferrite spinel structure [(Zn,Cu)Fe 2 O 4 ], along with trace Cu associated with insoluble silicate phases, establishes this ceiling under the applied conditions. Iron is a different matter. Its quadratic behavior is not merely a statistical artifact—it reflects a fundamental geochemical coupling embedded in the process chemistry. Fe(II) release is a stoichiometric byproduct of hydrazine-mediated ferrite reduction; every mole of ZnFe 2 O 4  decomposed necessarily sends iron into solution. This means that any operating condition aggressive enough to maximize zinc recovery will simultaneously drive iron co-dissolution, and no combination of the four variables studied here can fully decouple the two. The practical implication is unambiguous: an iron removal step—jarosite precipitation, goethite crystallization, or an equivalent—will be an unavoidable component of any industrially viable flowsheet built around this leaching chemistry. The linear structure of the Zn model reflects the operation of ferrite reduction as a single controlling step—a mechanism that responds additively to all four process variables without saturation or antagonism within the studied ranges. Copper’s quadratic behavior arises from phase saturation near its dissolution ceiling. The quadratic structure of the Fe model captures the multiphase origin of iron in the feed and the feedback introduced by iron reprecipitation at higher acid and temperature conditions.

It is acknowledged that the optimal acid concentration (1.0 M) lies at the lower boundary of the studied range, suggesting that a second-stage design centered on sub-stoichiometric acid conditions could potentially reveal weak interaction effects for Zn recovery not resolved in the present dataset. This limitation is recommended as a direction for future optimization work.

A full Fe phase distribution analysis, based on the Rietveld quantification in Table  3 , reveals that only 48.7% of total feed Fe resides in zinc ferrite (2.78 g Fe/100 g feed); the remainder is distributed among jarosite (1.37 g, 23.9%), goethite (0.94 g, 16.4%), and iron-bearing silicate phases (0.65 g, 11.3%). The observed 85.6% total Fe co-dissolution therefore reflects the combined contribution of hydrazine-mediated ferrite reduction alongside direct acid dissolution of jarosite and goethite—not anomalously low selectivity for ferrite-bound iron. The Fe/Zn molar ratio in the leachate (0.36, far below the 2:1 stoichiometric ratio expected from pure ferrite dissolution) is explained by this multiphase Fe distribution. This distinction has practical significance: downstream iron removal must accommodate both Fe 2+  derived from ferrite reduction and Fe 3+  derived from jarosite/goethite dissolution. A quantitative iron mass balance confirms the scale of this purification requirement: at the applied S/L ratio of 1:5 g mL −1 , the 85.6% Fe co-dissolution from a 5.71 wt.% Fe feed yields a pregnant leach solution Fe concentration of approximately 9780 mg L −1 —approximately 200 times the maximum tolerable Fe load for zinc electrowinning (≤ 50 mg L −1 ). The multiphase origin of dissolved Fe (Fe 2+  from hydrazine-mediated ferrite reduction; Fe 3+  from direct acid dissolution of jarosite and goethite) requires a combined iron removal sequence: an oxidation step (air sparging or SO 2 /O 2 ) to convert Fe 2+  → Fe 3+ , followed by either jarosite precipitation (pH 1.5–2.0, 90–95 °C, NH 4 +  or Na +  addition) or goethite crystallization (pH 2.5–3.5, 60–70 °C), both of which are established unit operations in industrial zinc hydrometallurgy.

Several features of these equations merit comment before turning to the response surfaces. The Zn model (Eq.  3 ) is the simplest of the four—a pure first-order expression in which  D  carries the largest coefficient by a meaningful margin, reinforcing the conclusion that hydrazine availability is the single most influential lever for zinc recovery within the studied parameter space. The Cd model (Eq.  5 ) is structurally similar but the sign pattern tells a different story: the large negative coefficient on  A  (−12.15) dwarfs all other terms, confirming that acid concentration is not just one factor among several for cadmium—it is the controlling variable, and its effect is adverse. The Cu and Fe models (Eqs.  4  and  6 ) both require quadratic terms, with the  AB  interaction in Eq.  4  capturing the coupled influence of acid concentration and leaching time on copper dissolution—a coupling absent from the other responses. Three-dimensional response surface plots for all four metals are shown in Figs.  7 ,  8 ,  9 , and  10 . The one-factor perturbation plots in Fig.  11 , generated at the optimized base conditions, provide a complementary view: they make explicit that temperature and hydrazine dosage govern Zn extraction through roughly comparable positive slopes, while acid concentration stands apart as the dominant—and inversely acting—control on Cd recovery. Multi-objective optimization via the composite desirability function, configured to maximize Zn, Cu, and Cd extraction simultaneously while penalizing Fe co-dissolution, converged on the following condition set: 1.0 M H 2 SO 4 , 6.3 wt.% N 2 H 4 , 85 °C, and 2 h. The full solution point and associated desirability value are reported in Table  7 . Three independent validation experiments conducted under these exact conditions returned extraction efficiencies of 91.7 ± 0.4% for Zn, 98.1 ± 0.3% for Cu, 91.2 ± 0.5% for Cd, and 85.6 ± 0.6% for Fe. The close agreement between these measured values and the model predictions—all falling within the 95% confidence intervals of the respective regression equations—confirms that the RSM models carry genuine predictive validity beyond the calibration data from which they were built. sections.heading: Characterization of Solid Residue under Optimized Leaching Conditions
paragraphs: Running the process at its optimized point—1.0 M H 2 SO 4 , 6.3 wt.% N 2 H 4 , 85 °C, 2 h—reduced the solid residue mass by 55–60% relative to the feed. That figure alone conveys the scale of bulk phase dissolution, but it says nothing about which phases dissolved and which did not. XRD and electron microscopy together provide that picture. The post-leach phase assemblage is markedly different from the feed. Soluble sulfate phases that accounted for the bulk of the feed mass have been largely consumed. What remains is a selectively concentrated refractory fraction: anglesite (PbSO 4 ), willemite (Zn 2 SiO 4 ), residual zinc ferrite (ZnFe 2 O 4 ), Mn-rich oxide species, and quartz. The survival of willemite needs no further explanation beyond the thermodynamic argument already made in the section " Thermodynamic Assessment of Hydrazine-Assisted Reductive Leaching ”—its dissolution is energetically unfavorable at any temperature within the experimental range, and acid strength alone cannot overcome that barrier. The partial persistence of zinc ferrite is a different matter. It indicates that the hydrazine dosage applied under optimized conditions was sufficient to decompose most, but not all, of the ferrite inventory. This is not a thermodynamic limitation—the driving force is unambiguously favorable—but a stoichiometric one. Higher reductant loadings would push conversion further, at the predictable cost of increased reagent consumption and a more demanding effluent treatment requirement. The absence of FeO or Fe(OH) 2  peaks in the post-leach XRD pattern is thermodynamically expected: the Gibbs free energy for FeO dissolution in dilute H 2 SO 4  is Δ G 5 0  = −114.4 kJ mol −1  at 85 °C (Reaction 5, Table  4 ), ensuring that any FeO liberated by ferrite reduction dissolves into the leach solution as FeSO 4  on a timescale much faster than the overall leaching experiment. Secondary jarosite precipitation is suppressed because hydrazine maintains Fe predominantly in the Fe(II) oxidation state throughout the run. A closing Fe mass balance confirms: of 5.71 g Fe per 100 g feed, 85.6% (4.89 g) enters solution, leaving approximately 0.82 g in the ~40 g residue—equivalent to ~2.1 wt.%, consistent with the EDS-measured 3.24 ± 0.45 wt.% Fe within analytical uncertainties. Residual Fe is attributable to incompletely decomposed ZnFe 2 O 4  and Fe incorporated within refractory silicate phases. The TEM micrographs in Fig.  12  tell a story that mass loss alone cannot. The feed consisted of angular agglomerates roughly 74 µm across, held together by intergrown ferrite, silicate, and sulfate phases. After leaching, those structures are gone. What remains are irregular fragments mostly falling in the 0.9–2.0 µm range—representative measurements of 953 nm, 1.21 µm, 1.66 µm, and 1.93 µm were recorded—with occasional finer debris below 500 nm scattered between larger pieces. A size reduction of more than one order of magnitude of this kind is not consistent with simple surface dissolution, which would round and shrink particles while broadly preserving their identity. It is consistent with structural disaggregation: the preferential dissolution of soluble sulfate phases and hydrazine-mediated ferrite reduction proceed along grain boundaries and interfacial defect networks, progressively undermining the mechanical coherence of the agglomerate until individual mineral fragments physically separate. The sub-500 nm debris is best interpreted as secondary fragmentation—material released when partially leached ferrite or silicate networks finally collapse after losing their load-bearing connections. Fig. 12 TEM micrographs ( a ,  b ) and HAADF–STEM images ( c ,  d ) of the leaching residue obtained under optimized conditions (1.0 M H 2 SO 4 , 85 °C, 2 h, 6.3 wt.% N 2 H 4 ), showing extensive particle fragmentation from the original ~74 μm feed to 0.9–2.0 μm fragments and the selective enrichment of refractory Pb- and Mn-bearing phases

It should be noted that the TEM-observed particle dimensions (0.9–2.0 μm) were obtained from dispersed powder specimens and represent a spatially limited sampling of the total residue. Bulk particle size distribution analysis by laser diffraction was not performed in the present study and would provide a statistically more robust, volume-averaged quantification of the fragmentation extent. However, the 55–60% bulk mass reduction and the near-complete dissolution of internal soluble phases confirmed by XRD collectively require that reagent penetration and structural disaggregation operated at the bulk scale rather than being confined to a fine subfraction. Laser diffraction characterization of leach residues is recommended as a priority for future process optimization studies.

Semiquantitative Rietveld refinement of the post-leach residue was not performed in the present study and is identified as a priority for future work. Qualitative interpretation of the post-leach XRD pattern nevertheless supports a mechanistically grounded prioritization of improvement strategies: the persistence of willemite with peak intensities comparable to the feed reflects a thermodynamic barrier (Δ G ° > 0 across 25–120 °C, “ Thermodynamic Assessment of Hydrazine-Assisted Reductive Leaching ” section) that cannot be overcome by adjusting hydrazine loading or acid concentration, and requires mechanochemical pretreatment or an alternative lixiviant system. The weakened but present ZnFe 2 O 4  reflections, by contrast, indicate incomplete but thermodynamically favorable ferrite decomposition that responds in principle to higher hydrazine stoichiometry or extended reaction time—kinetically accessible improvements within the existing lixiviant framework. Morphologically, the residue particles are anything but compact. They display irregular outlines, highly porous interiors, and rugged surface textures with clear evidence of inward-progressing dissolution fronts—in some cases leaving partially hollow or skeletonized structures where the soluble core has been consumed while an outer refractory shell survives.

The hollow and skeletonized particle morphologies represent internal pore networks from which residual process solution must be effectively displaced during washing—a challenge conceptually analogous to residual nonaqueous-phase liquid (NAPL) expulsion from porous media, where internal void geometry governs solution retention and release [ 32 ].

HAADF–STEM imaging (Fig.  12 c, d) adds a compositional dimension to this morphological picture. The pronounced Z-contrast heterogeneity visible at the nanoscale directly reflects the mineralogical diversity of the surviving fragments: bright regions correspond to Pb-bearing phases, darker areas to silicates and oxides, with intermediate contrast from Zn- and Mn-bearing material. Quantitative EDS analysis (Fig.  13 ; Table  8 ) confirms the bulk composition implied by XRD: Pb dominates at 33.59 ± 2.71 wt.%, followed by Zn (16.65 ± 2.0 wt.%), Mn (13.26 ± 1.62 wt.%), and S (9.00 ± 1.59 wt.%), with Si, Ca, Fe, Al, and Mg present at lower levels as signatures of surviving silicate and sulfate gangue. The apparent Pb enrichment from 11.80 wt.% (feed, elemental) to 33.59 wt.% (residue, EDS) is primarily a concentration effect: the 55–60% reduction in total solid mass retains nearly all feed Pb—immobilized as insoluble anglesite—in approximately 40–45% of the original solid volume. A simple mass balance yields an expected residue Pb concentration of ~28–30 wt.%, consistent with the EDS measurement within the combined analytical and mass-balance uncertainties. The slightly elevated measured value also reflects the positive bias inherent in HAADF-guided EDS acquisition, which preferentially samples high-Z (Pb-rich) regions. The trace element distribution deserves particular attention. Arsenic (1.2 wt.%), silver (0.2 wt.%), and zirconium (1.33 wt.%) all appear as reproducible EDS peaks, and their spatial distributions track those of Pb and Zn rather than being dispersed uniformly across the residue. This co-localization points to incorporation within the refractory oxide–sulfate matrix—structural substitution or surface sorption—rather than simple mechanical trapping. The consequence for downstream processing is favorable: these elements are immobilized in a chemically stable solid, reducing the purification load on any subsequent solvent extraction or selective precipitation circuit. Fig. 13 Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) spectrum of the leaching residue obtained from selected areas of scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) analysis, illustrating the characteristic peaks of lead (Pb), zinc (Zn), sulfur (S), manganese (Mn), silicon (Si), iron (Fe), and trace elements arsenic (As), silver (Ag), and zirconium (Zr) Table 8 Quantitative EDS analysis of the leaching residue, presenting atomic fractions, atomic errors, mass fractions, mass errors, and fitting errors for all detected elements Z Element Family Atomic fraction (%) Atomic error (%) Mass fraction (%) Mass error (%) Fit error (%) 8 O K 44.66 1.61 14.92 0.75 0.58 12 Mg K 1.02 0.21 0.52 0.11 2.05 13 Al K 1.04 0.21 0.58 0.12 1.21 14 Si K 7.62 1.37 4.47 0.19 0.19 16 S K 13.44 2.2 9.00 1.59 0.73 20 Ca K 1.25 0.17 1.05 0.15 0.49 26 Fe K 2.78 0.37 3.24 0.45 0.36 30 Zn K 12.2 1.48 16.65 2.0 0.08 33 As K 0.77 0.11 1.2 0.18 4.68 36 Zr K 0.76 0.1 1.33 0.19 3.27 42 Mn K 6.62 0.84 13.26 1.62 0.41 47 Ag L 0.09 0.01 0.2 0.03 3.82 82 Pb L 7.76 0.83 33.59 2.71 0.27

However, the long-term environmental stability of As, Ag, and Zr in the residue matrix has not been assessed by standardized leachability protocols (TCLP, EN 12457, or pH-static sequential extraction), and this represents a critical knowledge gap for any disposal or land-application scenario. Formal leachability testing is identified as a mandatory prerequisite for regulatory compliance assessment and is recommended as a priority for future work.

The immobilization of trace elements within the refractory oxide–sulfate matrix follows thermodynamic stability principles analogous to those governing impurity partitioning in pyrometallurgical copper refining [ 33 ]. Furthermore, the preferential attack along ferrite–silicate grain boundaries observed in TEM analysis is conceptually analogous to interfacial energy-driven phase separation at copper matte/slag/Fe 3 O 4  boundaries [ 34 ], and the presence of CuO within the (Zn,Cu)Fe 2 O 4  spinel solid solution may contribute to locally enhanced electron-transfer kinetics at the ferrite surface during hydrazine-mediated reduction [ 35 ]. Whether this concentrated refractory residue constitutes a viable secondary source of Ag or As will depend on the economics of targeted processing, but its existence as a defined, stable product phase is preferable to having these elements dispersed through the pregnant leach solution. From a resource recovery perspective, the Pb-enriched leach residue (33.59 ± 2.71 wt.% Pb) qualifies as a secondary lead-bearing material within the grade range routinely processed in secondary smelting operations (~25–40 wt.% Pb). Chloride leaching—exploiting the reaction PbSO 4  + 2Cl −  → PbCl 2  + SO 4 2−  in concentrated NaCl/HCl media—followed by Pb recovery via electrowinning or carbonate precipitation represents a technically viable downstream processing option for the anglesite fraction. A two-stage flowsheet integrating hydrazine-assisted reductive leaching for Zn/Cu/Cd recovery with chloride leaching for Pb recovery is recommended as a direction for future process integration studies. Stepping back, the combined XRD, TEM, and STEM–EDS dataset supports a mechanistic interpretation that goes beyond simple leaching efficiency numbers. The process does not work by dissolving a surface layer and leaving the particle interior untouched. It works by penetrating the agglomerate structure, selectively removing phases along internal boundaries, and physically dismantling the original particle architecture in the process. Residual zinc losses trace back to two specific targets for future improvement: the thermodynamically intractable willemite fraction, which would require mechanochemical pretreatment or an alternative lixiviant to address, and the incompletely decomposed ferrite, which responds in principle to higher hydrazine stoichiometry.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study represents the first systematic investigation of hydrazine hydrate as a selective reductive agent for the hydrometallurgical valorization of zinc ferrite-bearing cake residues from the AMMC production circuit. The findings span thermodynamics, statistical process optimization, and nanoscale residue characterization—three layers that, taken together, build a coherent and experimentally grounded case for this approach. On the thermodynamic side, the picture is clear. Hydrazine reduces Fe(III) to Fe(II) within the ZnFe 2 O 4  spinel lattice spontaneously across the full 25–120 °C range, with Δ G ° reaching −860.8 kJ mol −1  at ambient temperature and becoming more negative as temperature rises. This is not a marginal thermodynamic advantage—it is a substantial one, and it strengthens rather than diminishes with heating. Willemite (Zn 2 SiO 4 ) sits at the opposite end of the spectrum: its dissolution carries a positive Δ G ° throughout the same temperature range, which is why it survives leaching intact regardless of the conditions applied. No adjustment of acid concentration or reaction time changes this outcome; it is a thermodynamic ceiling, not a kinetic one. Process optimization via RSM/CCD—with  R 2  exceeding 0.98 and adequate precision above 31 for all four response models—converged on 1.0 M H 2 SO 4 , 6.3 wt.% N 2 H 4 , 85 °C, and 2 h as the optimal operating point. Triplicate validation experiments under these conditions returned extraction efficiencies of 91.7% Zn, 98.1% Cu, 91.2% Cd, and 85.6% Fe. Temperature and hydrazine dosage were identified as the primary drivers of zinc recovery, while sulfuric acid concentration acted in the opposite direction on cadmium—a consequence of selective sulfate precipitation at higher acid loadings that the model captured cleanly. Post-leach characterization added mechanistic depth to these extraction figures. XRD confirmed near-complete consumption of the soluble sulfate phases, with anglesite, willemite, residual ZnFe 2 O 4 , and Mn-rich oxides selectively concentrated in the solid residue. Hazardous trace elements—As, Ag, and Zr—were immobilized within this refractory matrix rather than migrating into the pregnant leach solution, which reduces the purification burden on downstream circuits considerably. TEM and STEM–EDS revealed that the original 74 µm feed agglomerates were broken down to 0.9–2.0 µm fragments through preferential intergranular dissolution rather than surface-limited shrinkage—a mechanistic distinction with practical implications for both leaching kinetics and residue handling. Two process limitations warrant honest acknowledgment.

The Pb-enriched leach residue (33.59 wt.% Pb) represents a valuable secondary resource amenable to chloride leaching for downstream Pb recovery, supporting a two-stage integrated flowsheet for complete zinc cake valorization. Residual zinc losses trace back to willemite—thermodynamically inaccessible under the conditions applied—and to incompletely decomposed ferrite, which responds in principle to higher hydrazine loadings. Mechanochemical pretreatment of the feed is one plausible route to addressing the former; elevated reductant stoichiometry is the more straightforward path to the latter, albeit at higher reagent cost. From an environmental standpoint, the process carries genuine advantages. Hydrazine oxidation yields only N 2  and H 2 O—no CO 2 , no problematic solid byproducts.

However, the upstream carbon footprint of industrial hydrazine production via the Raschig process (estimated 4.5–8.2 kg CO 2 -eq kg −1  product) represents a supply-chain-level environmental cost not captured at the unit-process level; a complete life-cycle assessment incorporating upstream reagent manufacture, process energy consumption, and residue management is recommended as a priority for future environmental evaluation of any industrial implementation.

Residual hydrazine in process effluents is reduced below the regulatory discharge threshold of 0.01 mg L −1  by H 2 O 2  treatment, a step that is both simple and effective. These characteristics, combined with the extraction efficiencies achieved, support a credible case for further development of this approach toward industrial implementation. From an industrial sustainability perspective, the sulfate-rich pregnant leach solution generated in this process represents a potential secondary resource stream whose valorization—for example, through electrolytic sulfur and hydrogen recovery [ 36 ]—merits future investigation. Effective process water recirculation and freshwater minimization, guided by water cycle management principles established for large-scale mining operations [ 37 ], will be essential components of any industrially viable implementation. Several experimental characterization gaps identified in this study represent priorities for future investigation. First, bulk laser diffraction analysis of both feed and post-leach residue particles would provide statistically representative size distribution data to complement the TEM-derived measurements reported here. Second, quantitative Rietveld refinement of the post-leach XRD patterns would enable precise phase quantification of the refractory residue components. Third, TCLP (Environmental Protection Agency [EPA] method 1311) or pH-static leachability testing is a mandatory regulatory prerequisite before any industrial deployment of this process, particularly for As, Pb, and Cd immobilization verification. Finally, dedicated reaction calorimetry for the H 2 O 2  neutralization step would provide quantitative thermal hazard data essential for safe process scale-up.
